title: Universal Robot Cone: Vendor-Neutral Keep-Out Zones
one_liner: One tap, or one cheap beacon dropped on the floor, creates a temporary no-go zone that every robot brand in the building obeys, with a log to prove it.
customer: 3PL and warehouse operators and hospital operations teams running multi-vendor AMRs, AGVs and autonomous scrubbers or forklifts, especially their safety managers and insurers.
problem: Mixed fleets each have their own fleet manager and zone tool. A worker who finds a spill, opens a lift or spots a person in an aisle cannot instantly stop every robot across vendors. E-stops are vendor-specific and incident evidence is fragmented. Existing standards cover fleet control (VDA 5050) or monitoring (MassRobotics), but neither provides a neutral, human-triggered safety boundary.
solution: Phase 1 is software: a tablet or wearable app that pushes a temporary keep-out polygon, with expiry and audit, to each vendor's fleet-manager API at once. Phase 2 is a $60-100 BLE/UWB and visual-marker beacon 'cone' that creates dynamic zones, with an open spec pitched to standards bodies. A neutral log records who created and cleared each zone and which robots entered it.
why_now: Multi-vendor fleets, many imported, are now normal in large warehouses and insurers say they are unprepared. VDA 5050 and MassRobotics adapters make cross-vendor integration feasible. ISO 3691-4 audits and rising incident claims give safety managers budget.
revenue_model: $300-800 per site per month for the software, about $75 per beacon, integration or certification fees from robot OEMs who want 'cone-compatible' status, and possible insurer premium discounts shared with customers.
non_obvious_insight: The safety stop line is the one thing every vendor must honor and the one thing no vendor wants to own across competitors. Whoever owns the neutral stop line owns the cross-vendor safety log, which becomes the reference record in any liability dispute.
first_30_days: Visit 10 warehouses running two or more robot vendors. Build adapters for two or three fleet APIs with open documentation. Run a paid pilot with one 3PL at $500 per month, used in a safety drill. Ask the site's broker for an endorsement letter.

title: Family Continuity Kit for Mixed-Status Households
one_liner: A done-with-you, notarized emergency-care package (standby guardianship, power of attorney, school and medical authorizations, wallet card and check-in alerts) for parents who could be detained without notice.
customer: Immigrant parents in mixed-status families, reached through trusted messengers such as churches, consulates, unions, clinics and schools. Co-payers: cities, counties and foundations funding preparedness, and employers in agriculture, meatpacking and hospitality. Price $49 to $149 per family, sliding scale.
problem: ICE issued Directive 11064.4 in July 2025 telling officers not to unnecessarily infringe parents' rights, but children still land in limbo when a parent is detained. The legal tools (standby guardianship, power of attorney, medical consent) are known, and nonprofits such as CLINIC and ILRC publish free guides. Execution is the bottleneck: state-specific forms, two-parent signatures, witnesses, a notary, and getting copies to the right person. California updated its guardianship rules in 2026, and city offices such as Chicago's 40th Ward publish emergency-plan guidance, which shows demand.
solution: A Spanish-first, WhatsApp-friendly workflow that interviews the parent, auto-fills the state's forms, and completes them through remote online notarization or notary-and-witness events at churches and clinics. Each family gets a wallet card with a QR code giving the designated caregiver instant access to the documents, plus school, bank and medical authorizations. Optional check-in alerts notify the caregiver and a legal-aid hotline if a parent misses a check-in. A caregiver checklist explains the first 72 hours. The forms are reviewed by legal-aid partners, and the app never collects immigration status.
why_now: Enforcement is at historically high levels in 2025 to 2026, and local governments are publishing family preparedness plans and updating guardianship law. Remote online notarization is available in most states, and messaging-app workflows reach families where they already are. Municipal and foundation budgets for know-your-rights work exist now.
revenue_model: $49 to $149 per family on a sliding scale. Municipal and county contracts to buy kits for residents ($25 to $40 each). Foundation grants. Union or employer benefit at about $5 per employee per year. Licensing to legal-aid organizations that lack completion capacity.
non_obvious_insight: For many immigrant families the highest-consequence legal document is not about immigration at all. It is a twenty-minute notarized form that keeps a child out of the foster system. Free guides exist but completion is low because the burden is witnesses, notaries, state variations and sharing, which can be productized. Payers exist beyond the family, since cities and foundations would rather fund kits than emergency foster placements.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a clear standby-guardianship statute. Have a legal-aid organization review the forms to avoid unauthorized-practice-of-law problems. Run notary-and-witness events at three churches or clinics and measure cost per completed family. Build the Spanish WhatsApp flow and printed wallet card, and design privacy so nothing about status is stored. Pitch one alderman's or county commissioner's office for a paid pilot of 500 kits.

title: TurkBridge: MTurk-Compatible Verified-Human Marketplace
one_liner: An MTurk requester-API-compatible endpoint backed by an identity-verified, proof-of-human worker pool, launched as Amazon Mechanical Turk closes on 30 Sept 2026.
customer: Academic labs and survey researchers, small ML data-labeling teams, and apps that use human-in-the-loop micro-tasks through boto3 or psiTurk-style code. Displaced MTurk workers are the supply side.
problem: Amazon closes MTurk on 30 Sept 2026 and the FAQ names no alternatives or migration path. New HITs end 30 Sept, bonuses are possible until 30 Oct, and transaction history is inaccessible after 28 Jan 2027. SageMaker Ground Truth and Augmented AI lose the MTurk worker type on the same date. Requesters have legacy code and no drop-in replacement, and quality was already collapsing because workers submitted AI output. One HN user says their app 'has been using Amazon Mechanical Turk for left-pad queries, and that service is shutting down in less than two weeks.'
solution: (1) Publish an API shim that mimics the MTurk requester operations (CreateHIT, ListAssignmentsForHIT, ApproveAssignment, qualification requirements, sandbox), so a codebase migrates by changing an endpoint URL. (2) Build supply from ex-MTurk workers on Turkopticon and worker forums, who lose income on the closure date. Give each worker a verified unique-person identity, passkey and liveness checks, and behavioural anti-LLM signals. (3) Sell two tiers, 'verified human' and 'domain expert', with paid-per-task quality gates. The product is the proof that a human did the work, priced above the old race-to-the-bottom rate.
why_now: The shutdown date is two days away, and worker income disappears the same day. Generic open crowd platforms have been wrecked by LLMs, so verified humanness has become the scarce good. Identity-verification APIs are now cheap (Didit, 'Stripe for Identity Verification', launched on HN in March 2026).
revenue_model: A 20-30% take on task payments, a $99/mo lab plan with participant-screening tools, and a per-verification fee for enterprise annotation buyers.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is trust in who is doing the task, and the API compatibility is what lets you take the customers. The MTurk FAQ confirms the dates and lists no alternative or migration path (https://www.mturk.com/help). In the 534-point HN thread (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49457545), dubeye writes: 'The problem as I see it is verifying the work is not done by AI. If it was possible to verify somehow that the work is definitely not done by AI I think there would still be a market.' Another user found MNIST accuracy from Ground Truth on MTurk 'marginally better than guessing.' Prolific is named as the maintained alternative, but I found no evidence that any alternative offers MTurk API compatibility. Legacy scripts are the switching cost, and the shim removes it.
first_30_days: Week 1: write the shim covering the 6 most-used MTurk operations, using boto3's endpoint_url override. Post a 'migrate in 10 minutes' guide on r/mturk, psiTurk and academic Twitter. Weeks 2-3: onboard the first 300-500 workers with ID and liveness checks. Recruit 5 lab requesters with free credits in exchange for case studies. Week 4: run paid studies, publish a proof-of-human quality comparison against raw MTurk data, and start charging the take rate.

title: Health-Check Weekends Abroad, Vetted by US Doctors
one_liner: Three- to four-day trips to Korean and Japanese comprehensive screening centers, with a US physician who prepares you before, translates results after, and coordinates follow-up back home.
customer: Americans 45-65 who pay cash for screening: self-employed, pre-Medicare early retirees, high-deductible households. The wedge is Korean-American and Japanese-American families who already fly to visit parents and trust the hospitals; the broader market follows.
problem: US preventive imaging and endoscopy are sold a la carte and priced for insurers: one whole-body MRI can cost $2,500, and an MRI plus CT plus endoscopy plus cardiac workup can run to several thousand dollars out of pocket. Korea and Japan built prevention into national habit, with one-day comprehensive packages (imaging, endoscopy, cardiac, labs) that reportedly cost 40-70% less than equivalent US screening, but US patients cannot navigate the language, the choice of package or the follow-up when they return.
solution: A packaged trip: (1) pre-trip telehealth visit with a US physician who picks an evidence-based subset of tests and avoids overkill; (2) land package with hotel, interpreter and escort at a vetted university hospital health-promotion center, results in days; (3) post-trip visit where the physician turns the translated report into a US action plan and books any follow-up at home. Group departures create cohorts and lower unit costs. Pair with the Workup Cover idea for the tail if a finding appears.
why_now: Consumers have shown in 2025-26 that they will pay $800-$2,500 cash for a single scan, and K-culture has made Korea an aspirational destination for Americans. Korean hospitals run international patient centers and take intermediary partners, and international screening packages are now marketed in English. US screening costs, high deductibles and the coming FDA and Medicare changes for blood-based tests are widening the gap.
revenue_model: Package margin of 15-25% (travel margin plus hospital partner commission where legal), $250 per physician consult (pre and post), and group or employer retreat pricing for early-retiree communities and small businesses. Optional membership for annual return trips.
non_obvious_insight: The right pitch is not 'cheap surgery abroad', which has a bad reputation, but 'join a country where prevention is a national habit'. The unclaimed value is not the discount but de-risking the two ends of the trip: choosing tests that matter and handling the follow-up in the US. The diaspora is the natural wedge because trust, language and family visits already exist.
first_30_days: Contact the international health-screening centers of three Seoul hospitals and agree one standard package and one heart-focused package. Recruit a telehealth-licensed US physician for pre- and post-trip visits. Recruit 20 pilot travelers from Korean-American church and community groups and longevity forums, take $500 deposits for a first group departure four to five months out, and get six seats confirmed. Keep marketing to screening and prevention, not diagnosis or cure.

title: AltSchool Without Buildings: Disability Programs in Host Schools
one_liner: AltSchool burned $170M+ building its own schools; in Texas, the new voucher money can only reach accredited schools with two years of history, so rent that eligibility by running clinician-led disability programs inside half-empty accredited private schools.
customer: Payer: Texas families with children on IEPs holding Texas Education Freedom Accounts (about $10k standard, up to $30k for IEP students at accredited private schools). Partner: small accredited private schools, often church schools, with empty classrooms. Supply: speech-language pathologists, BCBAs and dyslexia therapists who want to run a program.
problem: TEFA rules require private schools to be accredited and to have operated two consecutive school years, and microschool or learning-pod students get only $2,000. Families holding $30k accounts cannot find seats with real special-ed capacity. Eligible incumbents have buildings but no special-ed expertise. Clinicians have expertise but no eligibility.
solution: An operating company signs a host agreement with an accredited school. The school enrolls the students as school of record and receives the TEFA funds. We supply a clinical director, staff, structured-literacy or ABA-informed curriculum, IEP compliance, the annual norm-referenced testing TEFA requires for grades 3-12, and ESA billing reconciliation. Start with 8-10 student cohorts (dyslexia and autism support). Confirm with each host's accreditor that a program-within-a-school structure is acceptable.
why_now: TEFA's first year is starting (2026-27): $1B in funding, more than 130,000 applications in the first three weeks, roughly 100,000 families expected. Texas public schools lost about 76,000 students this year and are closing dozens of campuses. Federal special-ed enforcement was hollowed out (OSEP layoffs in October 2025, with the office reportedly moving to HHS in June 2026), so parents are looking for alternatives.
revenue_model: Management fee of about 20-25% of ESA revenue per student ($6-7.5k per $30k student, so $60-75k per 10-student program per year), with a 15-20% host share; one-time program-design fee ($3-5k) per host; compliance and reconciliation SaaS later.
non_obvious_insight: AltSchool's mistake was building schools. In Texas the moat is accreditation plus a two-year operating history, which are other people's assets, so partner instead of build. Empty church-school classrooms, underemployed clinicians and $30k accounts form a three-way arbitrage that only exists because of the new rules.
first_30_days: List about 150 small accredited private schools in DFW, Houston, San Antonio and Austin using accreditor directories. Send heads of school a one-page economics sheet. Recruit 10 clinicians via LinkedIn and SLP/BCBA Facebook groups. Sign 1-2 pilot hosts for a January 2027 cohort and collect pre-enrollment interest from TEFA parent groups. First revenue is host design fees, with per-student revenue starting once enrollments transfer.

title: GLP-1 Off-Ramp Program for Cash-Pay Prescribers
one_liner: A structured 12-week landing program for people stopping GLP-1 drugs, sold to the prescribers who lose revenue the day a patient quits.
customer: Independent obesity-medicine clinics, med spas and cash-pay telehealth prescribers (pay per enrollee); secondary: patients paying $149-249 for the program.
problem: Every fitness and nutrition company is building for people ON the drug. But real-world data suggest up to roughly 65 percent quit within a year, and a 2026 meta-regression finds about 60 percent of lost weight returns within a year of stopping (individual studies vary). The discontinuation moment is unowned: prescribers lose the patient, gyms never see them, and regain triggers shame and churn.
solution: A program keyed to the last-dose date: taper coordination with the prescriber, protein and resistance-training progression, weekly connected-scale weigh-ins, human coach check-ins on hunger and food noise, and pre-agreed re-start triggers (for example +3 percent regain) that route the patient back to the prescriber. Delivered by app plus partner gyms.
why_now: Oral GLP-1s at $149-299 cash (Wegovy pill launched Dec 2025/Jan 2026, orforglipron in April 2026) make starting cheap and stopping easy; about 1 in 8 US adults report currently taking one; cash-pay churn is the biggest leak in prescriber P&Ls.
revenue_model: $150-300 per enrollee paid by the prescriber as a retention and win-back tool (or $199 patient-paid), plus a revenue share on patients who restart therapy.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the prescriber, not the patient: the off-ramp is a retention product for the clinic's P&L, and a regain alert doubles as a win-back lead. Evidence on who regains is mixed, so a regain-risk model built from your own cohort becomes the proprietary asset.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 independent clinics or med spas, enroll 30 patients ending therapy using an off-the-shelf connected scale, messaging tool and a lifting template, and track 90-day weight, lean-mass proxy and restart rate versus each clinic's history to use as the sales proof.

title: Orphan Bin Network: Leased Farm Storage Capacity
one_liner: Lease the thousands of idle grain bins left on consolidated and inherited farmsteads, retrofit them with cheap sensors, and run them as licensed satellite storage for co-ops.
customer: Co-ops and independent elevators that run short of upright storage every big harvest. Also landlord and heir bin owners who receive lease income. The elevator pays a per-bin SaaS fee plus a share of storage revenue.
problem: Upright storage is the co-op's hardest constraint, and building new capacity costs a huge multiple of leasing existing steel. Ground piles cost shrink and quality. Meanwhile farm consolidation and aging landowners leave many bins idle on rented farmsteads. Heirs pay taxes on stranded assets and have no way to monetize them. Iowa law already contemplates leased storage facilities under a warehouse license (the licensee simply notifies the state), but no one has packaged the monitoring, inventory verification and paperwork to make it routine.
solution: A 'bin-in-a-box' program run under the co-op's existing warehouse license. Sign multi-year leases with owners and install a retrofit kit: temperature and moisture cables, fill-level sensors, aeration control and a remote camera. Wire it into the co-op's grain accounting system so receipts, inventory and shrink tracking work like any owned bin. Provide the compliance package (state notifications, insurance riders, inspection logs, an auditor-ready trail). This is not a marketplace. The co-op stays the licensed warehouseman and the bin owner becomes a landlord.
why_now: The 2025 record harvest left the top 12 corn states about 1.4 billion bushels short of upright storage, according to CoBank analysis, and low prices keep grain in storage longer. Elevators piled grain on the ground and rented temporary space. Cheap LoRa and cellular bin sensors now cost far less than a few years ago, and 2026 harvest is starting.
revenue_model: SaaS of about $250 to $500 per bin per year plus install margin on the sensor kit. 10% to 20% share of incremental storage revenue. Optional financing spread on kit costs.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not steel but licensed, monitored, insurable steel. Idle bins already exist by the thousands. What is missing is the trust layer (sensors, chain-of-custody and a bonded warehouseman) that lets an elevator sign for grain sitting in someone else's yard.
first_30_days: Pick one co-op that just piled grain on the ground. Identify 10 idle bins within 15 miles from the co-op's landlord and ag-lending contacts. Confirm the notification steps with the Iowa Grain Warehouse Bureau. Install sensor kits on 5 bins before harvest peak and store real grain for the first time this season.

title: Pickleball Noise Measurement Standard and Monitoring
one_liner: A court-defensible protocol, sensor kit and certification for measuring pickleball noise, sold to towns, HOAs and clubs.
customer: Parks and planning departments, HOAs, private clubs, court builders and municipal attorneys.
problem: Paddle impacts read roughly 70-80 dBA at 15 ft against 40-55 dBA ambient, and disputes are closing or limiting courts. In April 2026 a Missouri judge voided Kirkwood's restrictions as 'arbitrary, capricious and invalid' because noise could not be consistently measured. That leaves cities, clubs and neighbors all without an enforceable standard.
solution: A measurement protocol for impulsive, tonal sports noise (peak and Leq metrics, distance and background correction), a calibrated ~$500 sensor kit with cloud reporting and automatic compliance reports, expert-witness-ready PDFs, and an 'approved low-impact site' certification that helps at permit hearings. Add mitigation advice (barriers, quiet paddles and balls).
why_now: The Kirkwood ruling and hundreds of local ordinance fights, with participation at 24.3M and rising.
revenue_model: Kit sale or rental ($500 plus $30/month monitoring), $2-5k per-site certification, $1.5k expert reports, and protocol licensing to municipalities.
non_obvious_insight: Noise fights are fights over measurement. Whoever supplies the trusted protocol becomes the referee both sides must use, and courts have already said unmeasurable ordinances fail.
first_30_days: Contact 10 town attorneys and HOA boards currently in noise disputes and offer loaner sensor rigs. Publish an open draft protocol with an acoustical-engineer advisor. Aim for the first paid report in month one.

title: Municipal Trade Crews as Robot Training Data
one_liner: A cooperative that licenses consented, privacy-scrubbed first-person footage of city public-works and utility crews doing real skilled work to robotics labs, with revenue shared to the city and the union's training fund.
customer: Robotics foundation-model labs and robot-data buyers pay per usable hour (Physical Intelligence-class labs, XDOF, Mecka). The supply side is public works departments, transit maintenance shops and public-sector union locals (AFSCME, IBEW), which receive a 40-50% share.
problem: The humanoid bottleneck is a 'dearth of physical-world data'. Robot-data startups pay people to film themselves making coffee or fixing cars (XDOF at about $50M annualized revenue three months out of stealth, Mecka projecting $100M ARR). Those demos are shallow next to expert skilled-trade work in messy environments: valve exercising, hydrant flushing, pothole patching, streetlight repair, sewer inspection. Cities meanwhile face tight budgets and need non-tax revenue.
solution: Equip volunteer crews with head cameras and simple sensors for specified tasks. Scrub faces and license plates on-device, label task steps, and license clean hours under a contract in which the city retains ownership. Worker pay per hour and a union-controlled training fund keep labor onside. Later, offer 'task-specific corpora' by trade (electrical, plumbing, HVAC) via apprenticeship programs.
why_now: Robot foundation models raised at $3-14B valuations in 2026 and are starved for data. Data-as-a-service is the hot new category (XDOF, Mecka). The humanoid shipment wave (about 22,000 in H1 2026) creates immediate demand. Cities are under budget pressure (Maryland's new IT tax raised 77% less than projected).
revenue_model: Data licensing per usable hour and per task-specific corpus, with 40-50% of revenue shared to the city and union training fund. Enterprise annual data licenses for labs.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input for physical AI is expert skilled-trades demonstrations, and public works departments and their unions are the only large organized pools of trained workers with a single governance body that can sign one contract. Paying the workers and the union turns what looks like 'training your replacement' into a data dividend.
first_30_days: Find one mid-size public works department and one union local. Run a 10-worker, 2-week pilot with head cameras on two task types. Sell the first 300-500 cleaned hours to one robotics lab and pay the crews and training fund on the first invoice.

title: Documentation-Review Copilot for Notified Bodies and Labs
one_liner: Software that triages and pre-checks manufacturers' technical files for the third-party assessors that CRA, Machinery, radio-cyber and AI Act rules are about to swamp.
customer: EU notified bodies, cybersecurity and Common Criteria test labs and product-certification firms (10-500 staff), including newly designated ones.
problem: Third-party conformity assessment is required for higher-risk classes under several regimes: CRA important-Class II and critical products, the radio-equipment cyber delegated act, new Machinery Regulation duties from 20 Jan 2027, and AI Act biometrics (dates from background knowledge, verify). Assessor capacity is the bottleneck. Each file review takes weeks of expert time on incomplete, inconsistent submissions, and delay lands on the manufacturer's launch date.
solution: An intake portal that bounces incomplete submissions against a clause map, an LLM-assisted cross-check of claims versus test evidence versus SBOM, auto-generated clarification requests to the manufacturer, a reviewer workbench with evidence links, and traceable report drafting. EU-hosted or on-prem for confidentiality.
why_now: CRA reporting began 11 Sep 2026 and further obligations land 11 Dec 2027, while new-body designation and accreditation are slow. File volume is about to rise faster than assessor headcount.
revenue_model: $30-120k/year per lab, or per-reviewer seats at $500-1,500/month, plus implementation fees.
non_obvious_insight: In any permit regime the scarce resource is the assessor's hours, and manufacturers pay for delay. Selling to roughly 150 known assessors is easier than selling to 100,000 manufacturers, and it produces unique data on what a 'good file' looks like.
first_30_days: Email 40 labs and notified bodies and offer to pilot on a backlog of anonymized historical files. Run three paid pilots at EUR 5-10k, measure review-hours saved, and turn the results into a case study.

title: Hospital Back-Office Campuses Become Staff Housing
one_liner: Help nonprofit health systems convert surplus administrative office campuses, emptied by AI scribes and revenue-cycle automation, into staff housing, with the hospital itself as the master-lease credit that makes the conversion financeable.
customer: Nonprofit health-system CFOs and real-estate heads pay a fixed-fee feasibility engagement plus a success fee. Development and lending partners are secondary.
problem: Health systems own large billing, coding and admin campuses just as ambient AI (over 70% of large delivery networks have deployed or piloted scribes) and revenue-cycle automation shrink back-office headcount. Medicaid work requirements threaten 12.5-14.2% operating-margin hits, and replacing a bedside nurse costs roughly $55-60K by industry surveys. Meanwhile office-conversion lenders will not fund without a credit tenant, and 2026 rates are punishing.
solution: A 'space-to-housing' package: a utilization audit of admin real estate (badge, Wi-Fi and parking data), floor-by-floor conversion screening, a 10-15 year staff-housing master lease structured as a recruiting and retention benefit (rent by payroll deduction), tax-exempt or community-benefit financing, and a co-development partner. Fee at financial close.
why_now: AI scribes and RCM automation went mainstream in 2025-26, and Medicaid cuts force hospitals to monetize idle assets. Office vacancy is 17.8% with $39B of office debt maturing in 12 months. Public-partnered conversions such as 100 Gold Street (4,000 units) show a mission-aligned pipeline. PE physician-practice deals are down about 50%, so systems are holding more real estate.
revenue_model: $40-90K feasibility fee, a 1-2% success fee or development-fee share at close, ongoing asset-management fees.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce ingredient in office conversion is not design but a credit tenant. A hospital is the rare mission-aligned credit with a hard-dollar reason to want housing (turnover cost), and its own back offices are the least visible vacancy on the market.
first_30_days: Build a public-data list of 30 nonprofit systems with admin campuses (IRS Schedule H, county records, satellite parking counts). Cold-pitch a free two-page 'vacancy read' to their real-estate VPs. Convert 2-3 into paid audits within 90 days.

title: Polling-Agent Payroll With Proof-of-Presence Release
one_liner: Pay each party or observer polling-unit agent directly, releasing money only after a geo-fenced arrival selfie and a result-sheet photo, so nothing gets skimmed on the way down.
customer: Election observer NGOs and civic groups (donor-funded, need audit trails) first. Then campaign directorates of governorship, National Assembly and state assembly candidates across parties. Later, any organisation paying temporary field staff.
problem: Election day is Nigeria's biggest one-day distribution of small payments. Agent allowances travel as lump sums from state to LGA to ward to polling-unit coordinators. Each layer keeps a cut, so a N20k allocation often reaches the agent as N5k. Agents then no-show, or get bought by the other side. Campaign directors know this leakage exists but have no proof and no tool. Since the 2023 cash scarcity, everything has been done by ad-hoc bank transfers and screenshots.
solution: A WhatsApp, USSD and light-Android flow. The party or NGO uploads its INEC-submitted agent list. Each agent gets a wallet or bank payout. Payment is released in tranches: 50% on a geo-fenced 7:30am arrival check-in, 50% on upload of the EC8A result-sheet photo. A coordinator dashboard shows attendance heat-maps and unpaid or unresponsive units in real time. Payments are for presence and documentation only, never for outcomes. Amounts are capped and pre-approved, and a spend report is produced for Electoral Act limits. The platform is strictly non-partisan and serves any party on identical terms.
why_now: INEC has fixed the presidential and National Assembly elections for 16 January 2027 and the governorship and state assembly polls for 6 February 2027. Parties must submit polling-agent names by 10 December 2026 and 6 January 2027. The campaign season is open now, with the Electoral Act 2026 in force. Nigeria has roughly 177,000 polling units, and every serious party wants an agent in each. LLM-based photo checks and cheap bulk-payout APIs (Paystack, Flutterwave, Monnify transfers) make a small team viable. The deadline forces a fast pilot.
revenue_model: 2-3% fee on disbursed allowances, plus a per-agent onboarding fee of about N300-500. Campaigns and NGOs pay a flat SaaS fee for the dashboard and audit pack. Float on pre-funded wallets adds a small yield. After the elections, the same engine is resold as conditional-release payroll for temporary field workers: brand activations, survey and census enumerators, NGO vaccination and outreach drives.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer does not want digital payments. The buyer wants proof that the last person in a 5-layer cash chain actually showed up and got paid. Coordinators lose money to leakage, and that gives campaign principals a reason to bypass the middle layers. The wedge is fraud reduction, not fintech. A conditional-release payment is also more valuable as a workforce-verification product than as a payment product.
first_30_days: Build the check-in and photo flow on top of an existing payout API. Offer it free to one observer NGO or a single state-assembly campaign for a live Ekiti, Osun or by-election dry run, plus a paid pilot for a governorship candidate. Recruit 5 ward coordinators and get 500 agents paid in the first test. Approach NGO election-observation networks and donor programme officers, who already need audit trails. Get written non-partisan and INEC-compliance opinions from a lawyer before the first party contract. Price the first campaign at cost to get case studies.

title: Outage Pucks: Street-Level Blackout Cover
one_liner: A $25 plug-in sensor that proves your power is out and triggers a cash payout after 12 dark hours, turning neighborhoods of pucks into their own insurance oracle and a data feed utilities will pay for.
customer: Small food businesses (corner stores, taquerias, bakeries, daycares, ghost kitchens) and households with power-dependent medical needs (home oxygen, CPAP, insulin fridges, breast-milk storage). Secondary buyers are utilities and municipal resilience programs.
problem: Outage losses (spoiled inventory, closed days, hotel stays) are small and frequent, and today they are effectively uninsurable. Utility tariffs limit liability, homeowners policies mostly ignore off-premises power failure, and no address-level proof of an outage exists, so no product can pay automatically.
solution: A cellular, battery-backed puck reports loss of mains power with tamper detection. Outages are confirmed by cross-verification when several pucks on the same feeder or block go dark together, plus utility outage feeds. Payouts are $100 at 12 hours and $100 per additional 12 hours up to $600, with a higher medical tier. The anonymized street-level outage map is sold to utilities, regulators and insurers.
why_now: Grid stress from aging distribution lines, surging data-center load and public safety power shutoffs in the West is a live concern for households and small businesses. LTE-M hardware is cheap and instant-payout rails exist. CPC/IRI's September 2026 outlooks show a very strong El Niño likely, which means an active southern storm track over California and the Gulf and Southeast this winter.
revenue_model: Puck-plus-cover subscription of $8-$12 per month, with premium share to the carrier/MGA. Data licensing to utilities and grid-resilience programs, and grant or utility-funded seats for medical-baseline customers.
non_obvious_insight: Crowd verification lets a device fleet act as a parametric oracle at a resolution utilities themselves lack on low-voltage segments, where they often learn of outages only when customers call. The insurance product pays for the sensor network, and the sensor network is the real asset.
first_30_days: Buy 200 off-the-shelf LTE-M power-loss sensors and firmware-tag them. Place them with a restaurant association and a home-health agency in one storm or shutoff-prone metro. Launch as a capped 'outage guarantee' service warranty from the company's own balance sheet while an MGA is lined up. Pitch the aggregated outage map to one utility resilience team.

title: Demumu With a Body: Paid Welfare-Check Responders
one_liner: Parent-paid check-in safety for Chinese-, Indian- and Korean-speaking students and migrants living alone abroad, where a missed check-in triggers a paid local door-knock instead of an email to someone 10,000 km away.
customer: Parents (in China, India, Korea) of students and young professionals living alone abroad, who pay about $6/month plus about $45 per dispatched welfare check. Universities' international offices are a secondary channel.
problem: The viral Chinese app 'Are You Dead?' (renamed Demumu) proves demand for solo-living safety, but its only action is an email alert to two emergency contacts. For migrants those contacts are usually parents or friends in another city or country who cannot physically check. China has more than 125 million one-person households, projected at 200 million by 2030. About two-thirds of solo dwellers are aged 20-59, i.e. young migrants rather than the elderly.
solution: A student-controlled check-in app (student chooses the circle, parents pay). After a missed check-in, the escalation is: push, SMS and call, then roommates and landlord, and finally a vetted local responder who does a door-knock with a photo-verified report and can escalate to the local non-emergency welfare-check line or emergency services. The responders are recruited from the same student and gig pool as China's 'companion economy' providers, in host cities such as Boston, London, Sydney and Toronto.
why_now: Demumu's rebrand and global launch in January 2026 put the format on top of app charts in China and among paid utilities in the West, so users now trust the idea. Anyone can clone the basic check-in app in a weekend, since it reportedly cost about ¥1,500 to build. The defensible layer is physical response, which the viral app doesn't have. A 50 billion yuan ($7.4B) Chinese 'companionship economy' shows that people pay for on-demand human presence.
revenue_model: $6/month parent subscription, plus $45 per dispatch or prepaid packs of two. Later, university international-office licensing and insurer partnerships (travel and student health plans).
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the solo-liver. It is the anxious relative paying $30-60k a year in tuition, for whom $6/month is trivial. The viral product's critical gap is what happens after the alert. Evidence: Demumu reportedly cost about ¥1,500 ($210) to build, alerts two emergency contacts by email, most solo dwellers are 20-59, and there are 125 million one-person households (https://theconversation.com/are-you-dead-chinas-viral-app-reveals-a-complex-reality-of-solo-living-and-changing-social-ties-274536). It was the top paid app in China at 8 yuan and hit the top paid utilities in Australia (https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/1/14/chinese-app-are-you-dead-to-change-name-after-surge-in-popularity and https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-01-15/are-you-dead-app-changes-name-demumu/106228484). Companion providers already earn 3,000-5,000 yuan/month and one hiking firm grew from under 10 to 370 workers (https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/articles/hiking-hotpot-lonely-consumers-china-031456787.html), so a responder supply pool exists.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: White-label a check-in flow (Twilio plus a simple app or LINE/WeChat mini-program) and write parent-facing Chinese copy. Recruit and vet 10 responders (graduate students) in 3 cities, with a code of conduct and background check. Days 8-20: Post on Xiaohongshu 'studying abroad' and 'parents of overseas students' and in WeChat parent groups, offering a free first month. Days 21-30: Convert 100 parent subscribers, run at least 3 real dispatches and publish the anonymized outcomes. Test privacy and consent wording with 20 students, because the student must opt in and control the circle. Assumption to test: parents' willingness to pay, and student acceptance.

title: W-2 Employer-of-Record for AI-Training Experts
one_liner: A task-metered payroll, benefits and contract layer that lets data vendors and labs engage expert contractors as short-term employees without the misclassification and breach exposure of 1099 mass onboarding.
customer: Second-tier human-data vendors (challengers to the Mercor-scale players) and enterprise AI teams running expert-evaluation programs pay an 8-12% margin over payroll.
problem: A class action alleges Surge AI misclassified annotators, Mercor's reported breach exposed about 40k contractors' voice samples, and contractors report declining pay and stress. Enterprise buyers in banking and healthcare won't sign vendors lacking employment and security controls. Standard EOR services can't handle 2-40 hour micro-engagements.
solution: Instant W-2 onboarding across 50 states, with per-task hourly pay, automatic state paid-sick-leave accrual, workers' comp and unemployment tax handled. A data-security wrapper (SSO, ephemeral biometric handling) and portable pay stubs for the worker's income verification round it out.
why_now: Misclassification suits and breach fallout landed in 2025-26, enterprises are now buying expert data and demanding compliance, and a multi-million expert contractor pool has appeared with unprecedented scale.
revenue_model: 8-12% of payroll plus a per-worker admin fee.
non_obvious_insight: Leading marketplaces prefer contractor status because they keep 30-40%, but enterprise and regulated buyers can't absorb the liability. Being the plumbing for challengers, not another marketplace, gives them the enterprise wedge against incumbents.
first_30_days: White-label an existing PEO or EOR to avoid licensing. Sign two small vendors (legal, medical or finance data) for a pilot cohort of 50 W-2 experts. Publish a misclassification-risk checklist to generate inbound.

title: Executive Physicals for Union Trades Members
one_liner: Mobile 'Physical Days' at union halls and apprenticeship centers that give tradespeople the CEO-style cardiometabolic checkup, sold to the multiemployer health funds that pay their claims.
customer: Trustees and administrators of Taft-Hartley multiemployer health and welfare funds (building trades, Teamsters, food and commercial workers) and self-insured municipal and transit plans. First buyer: the fund of a 2,000-member electricians' or pipefitters' local.
problem: Workers 45-64 in the trades carry high rates of hypertension, sleep apnea, hearing loss, silica or dust lung exposure and undetected heart disease, yet they work 6am shifts and cannot make weekday clinic hours. Funds face rising costs (employers say GLP-1 drug costs loom large in the 2026 Business Group on Health survey) but their prevention is a voucher for an annual physical with low uptake. Corporate wellness vendors are built for white-collar campuses, not job sites.
solution: A 45-minute station circuit at the union hall or training center: validated blood pressure, fingerstick lipids and A1c (ApoB by send-out), single-lead ECG for atrial fibrillation, spirometry for dusty trades, audiogram, a STOP-BANG screen with a hand-off home sleep test, grip and gait, and FIT kits. A physician or NP reviews results the same day. Intermediate-risk members get a pre-booked $75-150 coronary calcium scan at a partner imaging center, and members with findings get a fast lane through a care navigator. Occupation-specific add-ons: sleep apnea for drivers, hearing and silica for construction. Fixed-fee pricing with no referral kickbacks.
why_now: GLP-1 spending has made plan sponsors receptive to prevention offsets. Point-of-care devices are now small and cheap enough to run a full circuit from two suitcases. Skilled-trades labor is aging and scarce, so trustees have a genuine interest in keeping members working and healthy longer.
revenue_model: $150-250 per participant paid by the fund, quarterly repeat days, plus optional shared-savings on downstream claims after the first year; add-on family-member days for spouses.
non_obvious_insight: Unions and multiemployer funds are the last pooled buyer with a 30-year time horizon on each member, so they are among the few payers who can actually capture the return on prevention (a corporate employer loses the employee after three years). Trustees are elected by the workers, so 'the same physical executives pay $5,000 for' is politically powerful. Elite prevention has to be sold where the payer keeps the member long enough to profit.
first_30_days: Get an introduction through an apprenticeship training center director or a local business manager. Offer a free or at-cost Physical Day for 40 members, staffed by a physician partner and two techs (roughly $6k in costs). Collect anonymized data on undiagnosed hypertension, high ApoB, apnea risk and hearing loss. Bring a one-page summary to the trustees at their next quarterly meeting comparing the cost of 30 physicals to one avoided cardiac event. Aim to sign a recurring contract within 4-5 months.

title: Gig Income Shock Cover From Pooled Data
one_liner: Insure the algorithm: pay drivers when they are deactivated or when regional platform earnings collapse, using pooled earnings data to defeat moral hazard.
customer: Rideshare and delivery drivers through driver co-ops, forums and earnings-tracking apps, and credit unions that finance drivers' cars.
problem: A deactivation or algorithmic pay cut can remove 30-100% of a driver's income overnight with no unemployment insurance, while record auto delinquencies (brief) mean many drivers carry stressed car loans. Individual income insurance has historically failed on moral hazard and adverse selection.
solution: A membership cover paying 2-4 weeks of trailing average earnings on (a) a verified platform deactivation, or (b) a regional earnings-per-hour index falling more than 25% against baseline, computed from pooled, driver-consented earnings data. Structure it through a fronting carrier or discretionary mutual, and offer credit unions a car-payment protection version.
why_now: Record auto delinquencies, growing algorithmic management of pay, driver data cooperatives and earnings-tracking apps that already pool consented data, and instant payout rails.
revenue_model: $10-$20 per month premium, credit-union-paid group premium bundled with car loans, and anonymized index data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: Moral hazard is the classic reason income insurance fails, but a platform-controlled event (deactivation) and a pooled regional index are not something the worker can game. The data cooperatives already exist and are the missing underwriting input.
first_30_days: Partner with one driver co-op or large forum for a 300-member paid pilot with a capped reserve. Collect earnings-data consents, back-test the index triggers on historical data, and have a fronting partner review the structure.

title: Original-Recording Music for Memory Care
one_liner: A playlist and licensing service for memory-care communities that matches each resident's favorites to the exact original master, and flags re-records, sound-alikes and AI covers that streaming catalogs are now full of.
customer: Memory-care and assisted-living operators (activity directors), adult day centers, home-care agencies and board-certified music therapists. Adult children pay for a family tier.
problem: Personalized music is one of the few low-cost tools that reaches people with dementia, but it depends on recognition of a specific, familiar recording. Streaming catalogs are riddled with 'greatest hits, re-recorded' versions, sound-alike compilations and now AI tracks. Deezer says over 50% of daily uploads are fully AI, and Sony has asked for 135,000+ impersonations to be removed. Understaffed activity directors cannot tell a 1966 master from a 2019 re-record, and facilities also carry public-performance licensing exposure.
solution: Intake asks a resident or family for songs, era, and where they danced or heard it. The software resolves each song to the original ISRC and audio fingerprint of the label master, rejects re-records, covers and AI-flagged tracks, and produces a device-ready playlist with the public-performance license bundled. Families can add human-made voice messages and personal recordings, stamped as verified human. Staff get a one-page 'response log' to note which tracks got reactions.
why_now: AI-track volume passed human uploads on Deezer in July 2026. Spotify, TIDAL and Bandcamp now label, demonetize or ban AI music, so machine-readable authenticity signals exist for the first time. Memory-care occupancy sits near a record 90%, the 80+ population is growing fast, and blood-test diagnosis pushes more families into post-diagnosis coping tools.
revenue_model: $99-199 a month per community, $12 a month for a family tier, and a per-seat licensing bundle where labels or collecting societies agree to a senior-living rate. Later, a B2B API for music therapists.
non_obvious_insight: In this setting the active ingredient is the exact recording rather than the song, and that is a provenance problem. The 'AI flood' harms the most vulnerable listeners because it degrades the catalog a caregiver assumes is authentic. The first pilot should test the hypothesis that covers and re-records underperform originals.
first_30_days: Build a resolver on public metadata (MusicBrainz, Discogs, label catalogs) and a fingerprint service. Offer a free 'playlist audit' to 10 memory-care communities and to Music & Memory-certified programs. Track staff-logged resident responses for original versus re-record and publish the result as your credibility asset.

title: Glasses-Free Zone: Smart-Glasses Detection Kits
one_liner: A detection-plus-policy kit for rooms where camera glasses cannot be allowed (exam centers, courtrooms, medical rooms, locker rooms, poker rooms), with logged, defensible procedures.
customer: Independent test centers, licensing and language-test operators, court administrators, casinos and poker rooms, med-spas, therapy and medical offices, gyms and locker-room operators.
problem: Camera and AI glasses look like ordinary eyewear and are now cheap and everywhere. Venues have bans on paper but no way to enforce or prove violations. In May 2026 two TOEIC test-takers were caught with AI glasses and banned for four years. The College Board banned smart glasses (even prescription ones) at the SAT starting March 2026, and New York State courts banned them across all courthouses in 2026.
solution: A door-frame or desk unit combining Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signature scanning for known glasses families, plus an optional optical check for camera lenses. It ships with a written policy pack, non-accusatory staff scripts, signage, a tamper-evident event log usable in score-invalidation or eviction disputes, and a short staff certification. The software updates as new glasses launch.
why_now: Camera-and-AI glasses went mainstream in 2025 to 2026, and other brands are launching. Institutions responded with bans in months, but incumbents (exam vendors, courts, gyms) have no tooling or procedures. The 18-month gap is between glasses in millions of faces and venue-grade controls. Consumer detector apps exist, but no one owns the evidence-grade, staff-friendly layer.
revenue_model: $299 to $999 policy and training kit, $1,500 to $5,000 per site for hardware install, then $49 to $149 per month for signature updates, incident logging and re-certification.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer's problem isn't detection accuracy, it's defensibility. A test center that cancels a score or a court that ejects a spectator needs a repeatable, logged, non-accusatory process to survive an appeal or a complaint. Sell the paper trail and the staff script, and treat the sensor as an accessory. False accusations, not misses, are what scare institutions.
first_30_days: Build a prototype scanner on an ESP32 or Raspberry Pi with known Bluetooth signatures from Ray-Ban Meta and other glasses, and test on real devices. Write the policy kit with an ex-proctor or court-security advisor. Offer paid pilots to 10 independent test-prep and test centers, one poker room and two med-spas. Charge for the kit from the start.

title: Chain-of-Custody Certificates for Spent PFAS Media
one_liner: A broker and tracking service that consolidates spent GAC and ion-exchange media from small utilities, routes it to verified destruction, and issues auditable certificates that document where the waste went.
customer: Small and mid-size water systems that have installed or are installing PFAS treatment, plus the treatment vendors and engineers who can bundle the service. Utilities pay per ton, and vendors pay referral fees.
problem: Step one: the 4 ppt PFOA/PFOS limits stand, monitoring is due in 2027 and compliance is proposed for 2031. Step two: treatment media saturates and must be replaced every one to three years. Step three: landfills increasingly refuse it, destruction capacity is thin, and utilities fear long-tail liability (PFOA and PFOS were designated CERCLA hazardous substances in 2024, from my background knowledge). The brief flags disposal as a downstream bottleneck but it is unverified.
solution: Start as a broker: aggregate small batches into full loads, match them to thermal reactivation, high-temperature incineration or newer destruction technologies, and issue a standard 'certificate of destruction' with custody records (tagged bulk bags, manifests, destruction-efficiency evidence and insurance). Sell it to media vendors as a bundled add-on. Later, add software for utilities' liability files.
why_now: Utilities that installed treatment after state limits and settlement money (3M and DuPont) are now hitting first change-outs. The delay from 2029 to 2031 moves the compliance date but not the disposal-liability clock.
revenue_model: 15-25% margin on disposal contracts ($ per ton), annual custody-software subscription and insurance-backed certificate fees.
non_obvious_insight: Regulatory relief changes when utilities must install treatment, not who owns the waste after it is installed. Buyers want absolution and paperwork more than the cheapest disposal, so documentation and insurance are the product.
first_30_days: Identify 10-20 utilities with early PFAS installs and imminent media change-outs from state announcements. Interview two disposal handlers and one reactivation vendor. Have an environmental attorney review a certificate template. Sign three pilot loads.

title: Laid-Off Auto Technicians to Water Operators
one_liner: A paid-placement training pipeline that turns displaced auto and machinery technicians into licensed water and wastewater operators.
customer: Contract water operators and small utilities, paying $4-8k per placed operator. State dislocated-worker and WIOA funds cover much of the tuition.
problem: Water systems face retirements, PFAS, nitrate and 2027 lead-and-copper deadlines with too few skilled operators. Meanwhile auto OEM robot orders are down 25% and autos lost 4.5k jobs in August, while the industrial maintenance and PLC skills those workers hold are what treatment plants cannot find.
solution: An 8-12 week bootcamp that maps PLC, pump, motor and controls skills onto Grade 1-2 operator exams plus PFAS media, ion exchange and membrane basics. Each trainee has a conditional job offer as an operator-in-training before starting. Solve the experience-hours bottleneck through contract-operator trainee slots.
why_now: Auto and metals layoffs are running alongside record capital-goods orders. Compliance clocks (PFAS monitoring 2027, LCRI Nov 2027) force hiring now, and EPA money for treatment is flowing.
revenue_model: Placement fee per hire from employers, plus state workforce-fund tuition reimbursement. Optional income-share for trainees.
non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint on water treatment is not money. It is people who can keep a PLC-run plant alive, and shrinking auto plants hold exactly those people.
first_30_days: Contact state Rapid Response teams for two Midwest auto-plant layoffs. Sign one contract operator for 10 conditional offers. Run a first cohort of 12 with a community-college partner.

title: Satiety Peptides for Small-Portion Foods
one_liner: Screen food-grade peptides that trigger the body's own GLP-1 release and put them in high-protein snacks.
customer: Protein bar, yogurt and snack brands serving GLP-1 users and people coming off the drugs.
problem: Small-portion products leave consumers unsatisfied, and CPG incumbents lack anything that helps portions feel sufficient.
solution: ML-screened protein hydrolysate peptides verified in enteroendocrine cell assays for GLP-1 secretion, supplied as an ingredient with structure-function claims only.
why_now: About 12% of Americans use GLP-1s, snack volume is shifting, and AI peptide prediction plus cheap CRO assays let a small team screen quickly.
revenue_model: Ingredient supply and licensing with per-kg pricing and development fees.
non_obvious_insight: GLP-1 drugs created a mass vocabulary for satiety, so food can compete at the margins of lower-dose and post-drug users without making any drug claim.
first_30_days: Hydrolyze two cheap protein streams, run an in vitro GLP-1 secretion assay through a CRO, and sample results to five snack brands.

title: Two A.M. Any-Tradition Rites and Interpreter Line
one_liner: A 24/7 dispatch of vetted ritual specialists and death-trained interpreters for families outside the majority faith, sold to hospices and palliative units.
customer: Hospices, hospital palliative units and nursing homes in metros with large immigrant and non-Christian populations. They pay a monthly retainer plus per-dispatch fees.
problem: Most hospice chaplains are generalists trained in a Christian or interfaith pastoral model, and chaplain FTEs are among the first things cut when margins tighten. When an imam, Hindu priest, Buddhist monk, Sikh granthi, Hmong ritual specialist, Orthodox priest, or Native elder is needed, the family often gets the default chaplain, and the ritual windows are short and unforgiving. Some rites happen only before death, others require that the body not be moved or touched for hours, or that someone be present continuously. Standard hospice protocol says 'call the funeral home now.' Language is the second failure. Family members interpret for the patient and quietly soften bad news. In many languages the word 'dying' is unsayable. Interpreter contracts are priced per minute and built for clinic visits, with no death vocabulary or truth-telling norm training.
solution: A dispatch line and app for the hospice chaplain or on-call nurse. It connects to a vetted, paid roster of ritual specialists by tradition and language who can arrive or join by video, plus a small pool of interpreters who have completed a 40-hour end-of-life interpreting course (death vocabulary, family-filtering, cultural norms about naming prognosis). A one-page 'rite card' library is loaded into the hospice's EHR or intranet for each tradition. It gives the practical do's and don'ts: how to position the patient, what not to do to the body, who should not touch it, how long to wait before calling the funeral home, and what the family may ask for. Start with one metro and 4 to 6 traditions.
why_now: AI translation is tempting hospices to cut interpreter budgets, while civil-rights language-access rules (Section 1557 of the ACA as revised in 2024) push toward qualified interpreters and human review of machine translation for critical content. Confirm the current status of those rules. The older-adult population is more foreign-born and religiously diverse than a decade ago, and the unaffiliated 'nones' need secular rituals too. Chaplain staffing is shrinking. Consolidated hospice chains want scalable ways to meet 'emotional and spiritual support' quality measures.
revenue_model: A monthly retainer of $1,500 to $4,000 per hospice or hospital for 24/7 access. Per-dispatch fees ($150 to $300 to the specialist, with a 30 to 40 percent platform margin). Premium per-minute interpreting rates above standard telephone rates. Training and certification revenue from the interpreter course, sold to language-service companies and hospitals. Family fees are not charged.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing is not spiritual care in general but time-critical, tradition-specific competence at the exact hour of death, which a generalist chaplain honestly cannot supply. Family interpreters are the largest hidden source of bad-news distortion in end-of-life care. Whoever builds the roster and the interpreter standard owns a moat that AI translation cannot cross, because the value is trust and ritual authority, not words.
first_30_days: Pick one metro where you know the communities (for example Minneapolis–St. Paul for Hmong, Somali and Karen families, or Houston or Queens for a wider mix). Recruit 20 to 25 ritual specialists and interpreters through mosque, temple and community boards, and pay them a small stipend for a 3-hour training on hospice basics. Build the rite-card library with their input. Sign two hospices to a free 60-day pilot on a shared phone number, then convert them to a retainer and use their case counts in a pitch to the next five.

title: Keep the 58-Year-Old Machinist Two Years Longer
one_liner: Carrier-co-funded ergonomic and assistive-tech programs that delay retirements instead of chasing new hires.
customer: Manufacturers with 30-300 employees and an older workforce. Workers' comp carriers and brokers co-fund it through loss-control budgets and premium credits.
problem: The industry chases Deloitte and Manufacturing Institute's 3.8M hires needed by 2033, with 1.9M possibly unfilled. Their 2024 report stresses retention, not just applicants. About 60% of manufacturing firms have owners aged 55+. Each retiring senior machinist takes years of tacit skill, and recruiting and training replacements is slow and costly.
solution: A 90-day Longevity Program. It starts with an ergonomic assessment of every role held by workers aged 50+. Then it installs a kit of lift assists, tilting fixtures, better lighting and vibration-damped tool holders, plus optional exoskeleton pilots for overhead work. It also designs phased-retirement roles (for example, mentor three days a week). It tracks injuries and retention against a baseline.
why_now: Manufacturing jobs are up 58k since the December 2025 low, so labor is tightening. Announced reshoring hires land 12-24 months after announcements. Lift-assist and exoskeleton hardware is now cheap enough for small shops.
revenue_model: $8-25k per program plus about $150 per employee per month for monitoring and a training-video library. Finder fees from carriers. Optional performance pricing tied to retention.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest hire is the one who does not retire. Insurers already fund loss control for exactly this age group, so the shop's cost is partly paid by a third party with a matching incentive. My rough estimate is that one avoided senior-machinist retirement is worth well over $100k in replacement, scrap and customer risk.
first_30_days: Call loss-control reps at three regional workers' comp carriers or brokers. Offer three free shop assessments. Document before-and-after injury and absence data. Use the results to sell paid programs to the shops.

title: Collateral Condition Reports for Farm Equipment
one_liner: Use newly opened Deere diagnostics to certify used-equipment condition for lenders and auctioneers handling a farm-distress wave.
customer: Community ag banks, Farm Credit associations, equipment auction houses and receivers.
problem: Farm bankruptcies are up 19% and row crops face a fourth loss-making year, so lenders are inheriting machinery they cannot value; poor condition data drives lowball auctions.
solution: An inspection product that reads fault history, engine and hydraulic hours and software status through independent diagnostic tools and issues a per-unit condition certificate, then builds valuation comps.
why_now: Deere's $99M settlement obliges it to open diagnostic and repair tools for 10 years, and repair restrictions cost farmers about $4.2B a year, so independent access is finally legitimate.
revenue_model: $250-600 per report, with annual subscriptions for lenders and per-lot fees from auction houses.
non_obvious_insight: Right-to-repair is framed as a farmer-savings story, but its most bankable use is collateral valuation for the lenders and auctioneers who must price distress.
first_30_days: Partner with three Midwest auction houses and two community banks, run 20 paid inspections using existing independent diagnostic tools, and publish sale-price comparisons.
